hook.text: Unhappiness has three parts: un-, happy, -ness. Each piece carries meaning. That's morphology at work.

buildup.text: Morphology studies morphemes — the smallest units of meaning in a language, like prefixes, roots, and suffixes.

discovery.text: Languages differ wildly in morphology. Turkish packs entire sentences into single words through long suffix chains.

twist.text: English is relatively simple morphologically. Mandarin even more so — relying on word order instead of suffixes.

climax.text: Morphology reveals that languages solve the same problems — encoding meaning — in radically different ways.

punchline.text: Meaning hides inside the smallest word parts.

quiz.question: What is a morpheme?
options: The smallest unit of meaning in a language

details.summary: Morphology studies how words are formed from smaller meaningful units called morphemes. Languages differ dramatically in their morphological complexity — some build single words from many morphemes that would require entire sentences in other languages.
details.whyItMatters: Morphological diversity shows that languages package meaning in fundamentally different ways. A single word in a polysynthetic language can express what English requires a full sentence to say, challenging assumptions about word boundaries.
takeaways: Morphemes are the smallest meaningful units within words
Languages range from isolating to polysynthetic in morphological type
Morphological structure shapes how speakers conceptualize meaning

faq.question: What is the difference between isolating and polysynthetic languages?
faq.answer: Isolating languages like Mandarin use mostly single-morpheme words with little inflection. Polysynthetic languages like Inuktitut pack many morphemes into single words that function as complete sentences. Most languages fall somewhere between these extremes.

faq.question: How does morphology differ from syntax?
faq.answer: Morphology studies structure within words — how prefixes, roots, and suffixes combine. Syntax studies how words combine into sentences. Languages that pack meaning into complex words (morphology) may need simpler sentence structures (syntax) and vice versa.
